routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Economics and Governance bachelor. Its two 24-EC thesis tracks, Economics and Governance, are equally formal and neither is named by the target. The Economics track appears first in the current official structure and is selected neutrally, independently of UCR fit.

audience.programmeDescription: Economics and Governance studies how markets, institutions and public policy shape sustainability. Economic theory, quantitative research and public administration are applied to food systems, environmental resources, development and energy transitions.
audience.comparisonExplanation: A complete comparison is withheld while the required natural or life science selection and applicable thesis-preparation conditions are verified. The supported curriculum is retained, with the science requirement separated from genuinely open electives.

provisionalCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
provisionalCourseDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

provisionalCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
provisionalCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
